name: Replication Through Removable Media
description:
Adversaries may move onto devices by exploiting or copying malware to devices connected via USB. In the case of Lateral Movement, adversaries may utilize the physical connection of a device to a compromised or malicious charging station or PC to bypass application store requirements and install malicious applications directly.(Citation: Lau-Mactans) In the case of Initial Access, adversaries may attempt to exploit the device via the connection to gain access to data stored on the device.(Citation: Krebs-JuiceJacking) Examples of this include: 
 
* Exploiting insecure bootloaders in a Nexus 6 or 6P device over USB and gaining the ability to perform actions including intercepting phone calls, intercepting network traffic, and obtaining the device physical location.(Citation: IBM-NexusUSB) 
* Exploiting weakly-enforced security boundaries in Android devices such as the Google Pixel 2 over USB.(Citation: GoogleProjectZero-OATmeal) 
* Products from Cellebrite and Grayshift purportedly that can exploit some iOS devices using physical access to the data port to unlock the passcode.(Citation: Computerworld-iPhoneCracking)

references.description: Brian Krebs. (2011, August 17). Beware of Juice-Jacking. Retrieved December 23, 2016.
Jann Horn. (2018, September 10). OATmeal on the Universal Cereal Bus: Exploiting Android phones over USB. Retrieved September 18, 2018.
Lau et al.. (2013). Mactans: Injecting Malware Into iOS Devices Via Malicious Chargers. Retrieved December 23, 2016.
Lucas Mearian. (2018, May 9). Two vendors now sell iPhone cracking technology – and police are buying. Retrieved November 17, 2024.
Roee Hay. (2017, January 5). Android Vulnerabilities: Attacking Nexus 6 and 6P Custom Boot Modes. Retrieved January 11, 2017.

telemetry.name: Application Permission
telemetry.description: Declared or granted permissions of a mobile application.
telemetry.collection_focus: Compare manifest declarations with runtime granted state using authorized package inspection and own-app permission checks.

providers.name: Android logcat
providers.scope: Permitted logs from a consented test device/emulator; output depends on build, permissions and instrumentation.

providers.name: Android dumpsys
providers.scope: Point-in-time service/package state on an authorized development device.

providers.name: Instrumented test application
providers.scope: Own-app permission, API and state callbacks; not universal visibility into other apps.

configuration: Use a disposable emulator or owned development device with approved debugging. Record OS/API level, app version and instrumentation privileges.
Collect only relevant logcat buffers/tags and service snapshots; add explicit own-app instrumentation for events absent from OS logs.
Forward sanitized logs and compare before/after state. Remove test data and revoke debugging access after the lab session.

configuration_example.label: Inspect the owned Android lab application
configuration_example.note: Read-only snapshot on a consented debug device. Replace the example package with your owned test app. Output and access vary by Android build; this is not a permission-request event stream.

telemetry.example_note: Project-normalized synthetic JSON, not a native provider log, captured event, attack verdict or validated detection. A parser/adapter is required for a real SIEM. Example names, IPs and values are fictional.
telemetry.limitations: Android tooling does not imply iOS coverage. Standard mobile apps cannot observe all other apps or protected OS internals; MDM status is not full API, filesystem or content telemetry.
telemetry.anomaly_design: Per owned device, app version and permission state: unexpected API/permission changes, background activity and network destinations. OS privacy restrictions and emulator differences limit observability.

telemetry.name: File Creation
telemetry.description: Creation or overwrite of a file at an observed path.
telemetry.collection_focus: Scope Sysmon FileCreate (11) to the lab directory; retain the process and file path. Differentiate creation/overwrite if the sensor can.

providers.name: Microsoft Sysmon
providers.scope: Windows event-based collection; enable the event types needed below.

providers.name: Linux Audit
providers.scope: Linux alternative for supported system-call and file events; different semantics and fields.

providers.name: Apple Endpoint Security clients
providers.scope: macOS alternative where the subscribed event exists; requires an entitled, approved client, not an iOS collector.

configuration: On a disposable Windows host, review the installed Sysmon schema and current configuration; merge scoped event filters into the existing policy rather than replacing it.
Forward Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational to the lab collector. Preserve event ID, timestamp, computer, process identifiers and the original event.
For Linux or macOS, select the equivalent sensor separately and test its emitted fields; a Windows event ID does not transfer across platforms.
telemetry.example_note: Project-normalized synthetic JSON, not a native provider log, captured event, attack verdict or validated detection. A parser/adapter is required for a real SIEM. Example names, IPs and values are fictional.
telemetry.limitations: Event filtering and sensor versions change coverage. High-volume image-load and process-access collection needs tuning; endpoint events alone do not establish intent.

telemetry.name: Host Status
telemetry.description: Host health and availability observations such as heartbeat, shutdown or degraded state.
telemetry.collection_focus: Collect agent heartbeat and OS health independently; record missed polls, last-seen time and monitor health.

providers.name: osquery
providers.scope: Scheduled host-state queries; supported tables and privileges vary by OS. Select a table that actually exposes the required object.

providers.name: Linux Audit plus inventory snapshots
providers.scope: Events explain changes; snapshots describe state at collection time.

configuration: Define the inventory query, allowed host set, interval and least-privileged reader. Store a stable asset ID, observation time and collector version.
Keep successive snapshots and calculate additions, removals and changed attributes. Pair state changes with audit events when available.
Export collector health and missed-poll counts so a missing snapshot is not misclassified as a missing asset.
telemetry.example_note: Project-normalized synthetic JSON, not a native provider log, captured event, attack verdict or validated detection. A parser/adapter is required for a real SIEM. Example names, IPs and values are fictional.
telemetry.limitations: Snapshots miss short-lived objects and do not identify who caused a change. A generic inventory agent is not guaranteed to expose firmware or kernel-level details.
telemetry.anomaly_design: Compare authorized state snapshots: first-seen drivers/services/modules, unexpected configuration drift and integrity changes. Record collection cadence; absence in a sample is not evidence of deletion.

telemetry.name: OS API Execution
telemetry.description: Instrumented operating-system API calls and their return values.
telemetry.collection_focus: Use an approved EDR trace or instrument the owned lab process at selected APIs. Define API name, caller, sanitized arguments and return status.

providers.name: Application audit logs
providers.scope: First-party service events and request/result fields; schema is application-specific.

providers.name: OpenTelemetry-compatible log pipelines
providers.scope: Transport and normalization of emitted records; do not create missing audit instrumentation.

configuration: Enable the application audit category or instrument the owned lab application at the authorization/action boundary.
Define a schema with timestamp, service, actor, object, action, result and correlation ID. Export structured records through an authenticated collector.
Redact secrets and personal content, separate audit from debug logs, set retention and verify delivery during rotation/restart.
telemetry.example_note: Project-normalized synthetic JSON, not a native provider log, captured event, attack verdict or validated detection. A parser/adapter is required for a real SIEM. Example names, IPs and values are fictional.
telemetry.limitations: Debug output is not necessarily a durable audit trail. Application developers must emit the relevant event; installing a log pipeline does not make an absent event exist.
telemetry.anomaly_design: Per application, client and route: request rate, rare actions, failure ratios and unusual state transitions. Version changes, retries, health probes and seasonal load need separate baselines.

telemetry.description: Creation of a process with executable, command line, parent and security context.
telemetry.collection_focus: Collect Sysmon ProcessCreate (1); preserve ProcessGuid and parent identifiers. Security 4688 is an alternative with separate audit/command-line settings.

strategies.name: Detection of Replication Through Removable Media

analytics.name: Analytic 1802
analytics.guidance: Defender correlates a causal chain where a device transitions into USB debugging or file transfer mode after a physical connection event, followed by application installation, file replication, or execution originating from the USB interface rather than the application store ecosystem.

tuning.description: Correlation window between USB connection state change and application installation.
List of devices legitimately allowed to use ADB debugging.
Approved enterprise apps allowed to install outside Google Play.
Volume of file writes from mounted external storage considered suspicious.

log_sources.name: android:MDMLog
log_sources.channel: device USB mode change (charging to file transfer / debugging / accessory)

log_sources.name: MobileEDR:telemetry
log_sources.channel: application installed from adb, sideload, or unknown USB source

log_sources.name: MobileEDR:telemetry
log_sources.channel: large file write originating from /mnt/usb or external mounted storage

analytics.name: Analytic 1803
analytics.guidance: Defender correlates a chain where a device establishes a new trusted USB host pairing or enters developer/debug configuration state, followed by device data extraction activity, configuration manipulation, or abnormal application behavior shortly after the pairing event.

tuning.description: Time window between trusted host pairing and suspicious device behavior.
Enterprise-authorized computers permitted to pair with managed devices.
Whether developer mode is permitted in the organization.

log_sources.name: iOS:MDMLog
log_sources.channel: Developer Mode enabled, supervised-device restriction changed, or trust-related protected device posture changed

log_sources.name: iOS:MDMLog
log_sources.channel: Trusted computer / host relationship established or relevant device trust setting changed

log_sources.name: iOS:MDMLog
log_sources.channel: Device risk, compliance, or security posture changes after trusted host pairing or developer-state transition

log_sources.name: MobileEDR:telemetry
log_sources.channel: Observed device-service, trust-service, backup/service interaction, or other privileged framework activity associated with physical host access

software.name: WireLurker
software.description: [WireLurker](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0312) monitors for iOS devices connected via USB to an infected OSX computer and installs downloaded third-party applications or automatically generated malicious applications onto the device.(Citation: PaloAlto-WireLurker)

references.description: Claud Xiao. (2014, November 5). WireLurker: A New Era in OS X and iOS Malware. Retrieved January 24, 2017.

software.name: DualToy
software.description: [DualToy](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0315) side loads malicious or risky apps to both Android and iOS devices via a USB connection.(Citation: PaloAlto-DualToy)

references.description: Claud Xiao. (2016, September 13). DualToy: New Windows Trojan Sideloads Risky Apps to Android and iOS Devices. Retrieved January 24, 2017.

mitigations.name: Security Updates
mitigations.description: Security updates often contain patches for vulnerabilities.

mitigations.name: Lock Bootloader
mitigations.description: Users should ensure bootloaders are locked to prevent arbitrary operating system code from being flashed onto the device.

mitigations.name: Use Recent OS Version
mitigations.description: iOS 11.4.1 and higher introduce USB Restricted Mode, which disables data access through the device's charging port under certain conditions (making the port only usable for power), likely preventing this technique from working.(Citation: Elcomsoft-iOSRestricted)

references.description: Oleg Afonin. (2018, September 20). iOS 12 Enhances USB Restricted Mode. Retrieved September 21, 2018.

mitigations.name: User Guidance
mitigations.description: Users should be advised not to use public charging stations or computers to charge their devices. Instead, users should be issued a charger acquired from a trustworthy source. Users should be advised not to click on device prompts to trust attached computers unless absolutely necessary.

mitigations.name: Enterprise Policy
mitigations.description: Enterprise policies should prevent enabling USB debugging on Android devices unless specifically needed (e.g., if the device is used for application development).

simulation.prerequisites: Use owned test devices or emulators, disposable app accounts and test data. Verify platform/version instrumentation; desktop test procedures do not establish mobile coverage.

synthetic.purpose: Collection/parser contract exercise, NOT a positive example or detection of this TTP.
